title: King Oliver record: Oliver's mute technique
summary: A King Oliver record is played; Barbarin recalls the Brunswick/Vocalion issue, his own drumming and how Oliver worked his mute with his hand.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: Let's play a record here.
What you going to play?
King Oliver, Sugarfoot Stone.
Oh, let's check for stop here. Oh, let's check for stop here. Mm-hm.
Where did you make this, Paul?
Chicago. What company was it? That was Vocalion. Well, affiliated with Brunswick, I mean.
Now it's on that Brunswick LP, King Olsen.
Yeah, it's on. Yeah. Well, that's the first time I've seen this over there. I didn't know there was an LP on there.
What's the drum on there? You hear that? Yeah.
Come over pretty good for the material I had at that time.
What kind of mute are you using there?
Oh, that's just a little bit of mute, I mean. I can't recall the name of that mute.
Does it look like a doorknob?
It looked like a doorknob, that's right. It looked like a doorknob. Yeah, yeah. Yeah.
How does he insert...
He makes the trumpet talk with you. He makes the trumpet talk with you. Yeah.
How would he insert that mute into his trumpet?
Well, he'd work his fingers and the mute together, you know. See, like he was playing the trumpet. Just like he was playing the trumpet, I mean.
Would he put it straight in or would he put it...
Yeah, he would put it straight in.
He'd put it straight in?

Straight in, yeah. And he'd work it in and out like that, you know. And sometimes he would keep it in and he'd work his hand, you see. Would he hold it? He'd work it and close his hand, you see. Yeah. Close his hand, you see. And he'd use it that way, you see.
Would he hold his hand up? Would he grab the mute with his hand like that?

Yeah, like that. All around, huh? Like that. He'd open his fingers, yeah. He'd open his fingers, but no, he wouldn't pull the mute all the way out. Not far, not far, say about five or six inches, I mean, in the back end again. Not way out, you know what I mean? He never did that. That's a pretty good record. No record sound that good. That's a nice record. I mean, for the time of the record.
